rules.statement: A reusable OpenTofu component module declares its `required_providers` but contains no `provider` configuration block and no `backend` block.
rules.why: Provider and backend configuration belong to the composition root (stack or live configuration), so the component can be reused in any environment.
rules.check: Look for `provider "..." {}` blocks or `terraform { backend ... }` inside a component module directory rather than a stack or live configuration.

rules.statement: A reusable infrastructure component takes its dependencies as input variables and exposes what others need as outputs, and doesn't look up another component's resources itself through data sources or remote state.
rules.why: Lookups across components couple them and break composition; stacks wire components together explicitly.
rules.check: Look for `data` sources or `terraform_remote_state` in a component that fetch resources another component creates, instead of taking them as variables.

rules.statement: Every reusable infrastructure component ships a README, an example, and `tofu test` tests that use mocked providers.
rules.why: Components are published products that other people consume and get support for, so they need documentation and tests that run without real cloud credentials.
rules.check: Check that a new or changed component directory has a README, an example, and `*.tftest.hcl` tests that use `mock_provider`.

rules.statement: Treat an infrastructure component's variables and outputs as its public API: removing or renaming a variable or output, adding a required input, or forcing a resource replacement is a breaking change that needs a major version.
rules.why: Consumers pin released versions and have to act on these changes.
rules.check: Look for removed or renamed variables or outputs, new variables without defaults, or changes that force resource replacement, where the diff doesn't flag the change as breaking.

rules.statement: When a refactor of an infrastructure component renames, moves or drops resources, it uses `moved` and `removed` blocks so that existing state isn't destroyed and recreated.
rules.why: Without these blocks, consumers who upgrade get forced resource replacements.
rules.check: Look for a resource address that was renamed, moved into or out of a module, or deleted, where the diff has no matching `moved` or `removed` block.

rules.statement: Reusable infrastructure components declare provider version ranges, not exact versions; exact provider versions are pinned only by the lock file of the deployed live configuration.
rules.why: Exact pins in shared components conflict across consumers; the live configuration owns the exact versions it runs.
rules.check: Look for exact `version = "x.y.z"` provider constraints in component or stack code, or a lock file committed outside the live configuration.

rules.statement: Live deployment configuration references reusable infrastructure modules and stacks only by a released version, pinned by digest where the source supports it, never by a local path or a branch.
rules.why: The hosted deployment has to exercise exactly the published artifacts that self-hosters consume.
rules.check: Look for `source = "../..."`, local paths, or unpinned branch refs in live or cluster configuration.

rules.statement: Reusable deployment components, stacks and charts take environment-specific values (domains, hostnames, account IDs, secret or parameter-store paths) as inputs and don't hard-code them or default them to the vendor's own environment.
rules.why: Published artifacts have to stay generic for self-hosters; platform specifics belong only in the live configuration.
rules.check: Look for variable defaults, or literals in component, stack or chart code, that name a specific production domain, hostname, account or SSM path.

rules.statement: A reusable infrastructure component is secure by default: its default input values pick the secure configuration.
rules.why: Components are published for other people to use, so a configuration that takes the defaults must be safe.
rules.check: Look for defaults that open public access, turn off encryption or TLS, or grant broad permissions unless the consumer opts in.
